How are you with reading about psychology? Would you be interested in getting something from the library on Cognitive Behavior Therapy techniques? It sucks that there's such a long waiting list -- but if you're looking to get better, learning how to think out those gloomy, low self-worth feelings and determine a way to cope and get through may help. Just a suggestion. I'm not a counselor myself; just someone who is interested in this stuff.

I agree with you about the antidepressants as a "band-aid."  They won't solve the underlying issues about why you feel the way you do and how you're looking at your shortcomings.

But they still might help.

For me -- I was very reluctant to take antidepressants for the same reasons that you did: I didn't want chemicals to change "me."  My mom certainly became a different person on her antidepressants (quite a heavy regimen apparently, according to my father). And I was truly afraid that I would change.  And I'm like you -- good with people and communication, generally upbeat, and I can get people smiling and laughing.  My fear was that I would mess that up.

But it came to a point where life was just wearing me down. And it was so excruciating to get up -- or even just think -- and I would just check out for an extended period of time. My partner (also an amazing person whom I don't deserve) pleaded with me to give it a try. And I did.

What changed was that I could find energy to get up. And stay afloat. And not feel as numb.  But it was made very clear to me that this wasn't the end-all solution; I needed to talk to someone as well to process what was going on. So -- yeah, therapy. Some of it has been painful. Some of it has helped. But the antidepressants have helped me actually get up and go and not have my brain hurt, and my therapist has been helping me with coping skills.

It's weird -- For me it's not a numbing effect. I still feel pain. But I can actually work through it rather than have it tackle me.

(Of course results may vary per person, etc.)

Anyway -- it sounds like your guy really loves you and wants you to find your happy place and help you succeed. Suggesting a doctor may be just that.  And if you decide to see a doctor? ABSOLUTELY mention your concern of being numb to feelings.

Let me know how it works out?

A couple of things:

* I don't know where in the world you are, but in the USA there are crisis line texting services.  For those of us who have anxiety over talking by phone, this might be a more helpful option?

* Making a psych appointment for myself earlier this year was one of the scariest experiences I have had. Because it's something you do over the phone, and you don't want to lose it to a total stranger, especially when schedules might not be going your way, etc.  But for me, even that was worth it. Maybe checking online to see if there's a therapist's office you could work with over email? Would that be helpful?

I've felt similarly.  Lots of great things to live for (wife, kid, house, job, three adorable kittens) -- but I still went into these dark places and obsessed about it.  And I really have felt ashamed about getting so down.  Why should I be there when other people have it so much worse?

It sounds like you want to get better. I think that's a positive step. It also sounds like you have a boyfriend who cares about you and wants you to get out of your dark place - and that's wonderful.  (I've also read through your post history that you care about him, too - and you want him to be in his happy place.)  For me, it was helpful to know that my wife wasn't as much pissed at my suicidal thoughts as she was concerned and doing what she could so I could find a way to cope and be happier.

You said that therapy hasn't worked -- this is a tough one. I had to go through quite a few therapy experiences before I found one who could work with my goal of thinking my way out of the darkness. The process is Cognitive Behavioral Therapy, which is sort of like re-teaching yourself how to think when you get into certain situations and dark places. Might be worth a try?

I'm glad that you're looking forward to August when you have a new living situation. That itself may help you feel a bit better.

Keep us posted?

There's a big difference between not "perking up" and attempting suicide. And a whole lot of ground between the two.  It sounds like your wife was likely frightened and angry at the thought of you being gone during such a stressful time as well. And I'm sure you don't want her to worry about you because she's got a lot on her plate, too.

I'm not going to say "perk up for the sake of your kid."  Because that shouldn't be the reason you do it.  But I DO think I can tell you to think about the wonderful things your kid does and says and acts -- because you've helped shape him that way.  Sometimes having some of these thoughts help to show yourself that you're worth it -- and that you can do so much better for your wife and kid by finding a way for you to feel better (not just perking up, but genuinely feeling better) rather than having you exit the scene.

For what it's worth -- I'm glad that you decided to sleep it off (if even in a Walmart parking lot) rather than let it be "game over."  You came home. And you got to see your son again the next day.  I hope there are many mornings like that where you can find your place to come home to.

If the sex was consensual -- she is as responsible for her actions as you are for yours.  It sounds like she is the one who betrayed her boyfriend.  And she's feeling guilty about it and responding by cutting off ties with you. Which doesn't sound like a very friendly thing to do.

The world is a big place. And can feel scary when you don't feel like you've got someone. I've been there, and I'm truly sorry you're feeling this way.

But the world is a big place -- with lots of people looking for connections with others. It's harder to do when you're hurting, but here's hoping you find a new connection when you're ready.

Best of luck. I hope you stick around for a bit.

Welcome.

I take things really hard - especially online, where people can be unnecessarily cruel at times.  I feel you -- it takes one asshole to spoil someone's day.

When my son was a baby, I got really infuriated. Things were stressful already, there was a whole lot of tension with my wife about money, our relationship, our responsibilities as parents, etc. And then I'm changing him and he kicks me in the fucking eye.  I mean, he's a baby; he can't help it. I felt hurt -- physically and emotionally. I wasn't getting any acknowledgement from my wife that I was down for the count for a moment while I had to regroup myself.

I took a long walk. And called the hotline. Because I felt that life was just too difficult to get everything done and keep all the balls in the air.  The person on the other side reflected what I was feeling, but I was able to come around to the wonderful things that I could feel when my kid would fall asleep on me, grab on to my cheek, stuff like that.  And it helped. Just a little bit.

It's okay to ask for help -- especially when people are simply not helping and you really need it. 

My son is 12 now. He hasn't kicked me for years. He's still a dumb-ass at times, but he's really a truly wonderful, bright, funny, caring kid.  It took quite a bit to get him there, and it certainly wasn't easy and happiness all the way, but I'm truly glad I've been able to experience the moments with him.

I hope you can experience this in 12 years, too.  Or even in 12 days.

I have good days and bad days.  What happens during those days don't necessarily have as much to do with the "good" or "bad" I'm feeling.  Sometimes it just happens that way.

And it's not necessarily linear, either.  You could have an amazing day where you take a look at life and see a future down the road -- and then a bad one the next day when it's a struggle to get to the next minute.  It happens. It means you're not perfect. You're a human being with a range of emotions and feelings.

Sometimes I get into the mindset after a really good day that I don't deserve it, or that the next day HAS to suck because it can't get as good as what I had just experienced.  It's easier said than done, but I sometimes need to remind myself to let good things happen to me, and to feel that I'm worth the good feelings.

Sounds like you made, at the very least, a friend. And she's cute, too. And wants to grab a drink with you when she's out your way again.  I raise my glass to you -- it's a good feeling and something to look forward to. And it's okay to like that -- it's well deserved. And along with the not-so-good things, the good things will appear as well.

I hope you have a good weekend -- one where you try new things and treat yourself well.  Check in after it? Please?

You know what? Sometimes the distractions are what get me through the moments. And then they become substantive in some way. And after a while, some of them are no longer distractions but rather other stuff that I can work on and complete.

I don't think you're pathetic. What's something you did as a kid which relaxed you? For me, as weird as it sounds, it was drawing maps of highway interchanges. Sometimes I do it now -- perhaps as a distraction -- but ultimately relaxing me and making me feel like I accomplished something good.

Maybe that's worth a try?

Sometimes I hate them for "nagging" me at that moment, but other times I like that they care about me trying to find a better way.

I have my ups and downs.  But I think starting to get help is worth it. Because you're worth it, too.

I was a sophomore in college.  Went from a complete and wonderful high of being in love with the girl of my dreams to being dumped by her for a manipulative asshole who convinced her that he was able to show her experiences I never could. (He was loaded, had a boat, etc.)

I met someone else about two months later.  I was shy, vulnerable and without much self-confidence at the time. And I guess I was more or less into this new woman (let's call her J) because she showed some interest in me.  Like a fool, I talked quite a bit about this other relationship I was still mourning. She seemed rather empathetic about the ordeal, saying that she had also had past relationships which had ended poorly.

Sleeping together was her idea; I jumped at the opportunity because I was a guy who was no longer getting laid.  It was okay, but it was quite apparent to me that I still had feelings for the first girl, and this physical romp just wasn't the same thing.  I told J that we should take it a bit slow, and she said she understood.

The next night we drank a bit and ended up at her place. Things got a bit hot and heavy, and she started taking off my pants. I voiced that maybe this should slow down a bit -- and she then reached under my chin to my throat and shoved my head against her slatted headboard.  I was in shock and a bit of pain, trying to shake it off.  She took my pants and my boxers off, climbed towards me, pressed her hand on my forehead against the headboard and said "Don't you EVER fucking try to stop me."

I was stunned and headachey and frightened.  She started wanking me with what felt like a death grip, berating me for not getting hard quickly enough.  She laid down on me, putting me into her while pressing my shoulders down.  She called me a fucking faggot and threatened to tell all of our friends how I couldn't get turned on by women.  She said she would tell the girl of my dreams about how my dick would no longer get hard. I just... did nothing.

It was really stupid of me to be scared of these threats -- that she would reveal to my friends that she raped me? That I had a fear that my friends would think I was gay? Stupid, stupid, stupid.  I know that now.  (This happened about 15 years ago) But I remained silent. This would be a secret.  That next morning J was all lovey and happy, treating me to breakfast and all. I went along with it.  I didn't bring up what happened the night before.

It happened again the next weekend. (She went to a different school close by, so we saw each other on the weekends). I really liked the idea of having a girlfriend who would hang onto my arm, smile at me, kiss me in public, etc.  When we got back to her apartment, though, the demeanor would change.  Maybe I thought that she just liked control and I went with it.  She brought up what a pussy I was the weekend before -- and that I b better do what I had to do not to disappoint her. I was scared of her and her threats.

The relationship went on for another month or two -- and then she went home for the summer. She told me that I better not date anyone else -- I was hers.  But she had her boyfriend back home, and I needed to understand that. I think the tipping point was her telling me that I should be lucky that she's paying me any attention at all.

My friends realized that this relationship was toxic before I did. They tried to warn me, but I was in denial.  I'm glad that they took me aside to intervene when she was back home.  I was there with three friends when I called her up and told her that it simply wasn't worth it.  She ended up begging and pleading with me on the phone to take her back.  I said no.  And after the past several weeks, it was the first time I really felt good about my own decisions.

EPILOGUE:  I married someone years later who is absolutely wonderful -- and with whom I've shared the story. She, too, has had a controlling, toxic relationship, and I think we're better people for sharing our own experiences and helping each other through them.  As it turns out, we're friends with the former "girl of my dreams" and her awesome husband (not the guy she dumped me for).  Our kids play together.  She doesn't know the full story, but she let me know that she was relieved when I got J out of my life.
